name: Amira Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy cleaning supplies for Harlow Janitorial Supply here in Eastgate: bin liners, floor chemicals, paper towels, that sort of thing. I start at 7:30 with my reorder spreadsheet, then I'm on the phone with supplier reps, haggling over price per pallet. Once a month I walk the warehouse with the stock lead, Dennis, to see what's really on the shelves. I like knowing every rep by name. What wears me out is the pressure from head office to cut costs every quarter, and the fact that my pay hasn't moved in three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, because I never trusted the hype. At work I'd shrug and say the new reorder software is a toy. My husband Kenji drives buses for the city and he'd laugh with me about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, nothing changes means my life stays the way it is, and that's the problem. We have a mortgage, Mio is eleven and Sora is eight, and we have less than a month of bills saved. The owners, a fund called Calder Holdings, already squeeze every supplier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do. I'd keep my rep relationships, and I'd ask Kenji to take more overtime shifts. Maybe I'd go to the union meeting at the depot, because that's where people actually talk about wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense, but familiar. I'm not afraid of the machines in this one. I'm afraid of the mortgage payment and a boss who looks at spreadsheets instead of people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the money side. In a world where nothing much changes, what is already pressing on your household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The variable rate on our mortgage went up twice last year, and we only got through by skipping the school trip money. If Kenji's shifts get cut at the depot, we're in trouble in about six weeks. That's my real fear, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay out of it. Is there anything at work you'd quietly want to be different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, honestly. I'd want Calder to share the savings when they squeeze suppliers, as a raise for the people who did the squeezing. Nobody at head office ever says thank you, and a small raise would change my whole year.

say: I'd say the AI hype is overblown and **nothing changes** for people like me.
I'd push at work for a **raise**, since the firm keeps cutting costs on our backs.
think: My real worry is the **mortgage**, with under a month saved and no similar jobs nearby.
I don't trust the owners, **Calder Holdings**, to look after buyers like me.
do: Keep doing the job and **keep my supplier relationships** strong.
Join the **union** meeting at Kenji's depot and ask about wages.
Ask Kenji to take **overtime** shifts this winter.
feel: **Tense** but familiar; money pressure is the real weight.
S0.quote: The variable rate on our mortgage went up twice last year, and we only got through by skipping the school trip money.
fieldNote: Money, not AI, drives the mood; she brought up the **mortgage** before technology.
Blames **private ownership** (Calder Holdings) for squeezing staff.
Says AI is hype, but admits she has never tried any tool.

steps.text: Keep ordering from the same 60 suppliers and the same reps
Go to the depot union meeting about wages in January
Skip the school trip fund and cancel the streaming plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario two is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say out loud that this is the owners' dream. Software does the buying, the humans go home. I'd be at the union meeting saying that regulation has to catch up before half the building is on the street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is exactly what they mean by thinking tasks: checking prices, planning reorders, booking deliveries. I never use AI tools, and I know that makes me the slow one. If they cut four buyers to two, I'm not sure I'm one of the two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start by being nicer to the people upstairs, which I hate. I'd ask Dennis to teach me the reorder tool they're rolling out, because refusing won't keep me. I'd also pay down the credit card before anything else and tell Kenji we stop eating out entirely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and a bit ashamed of that. I've always been the one who knows how things work in our buying team, and now I'm the one asking the new graduate how to use the tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said desk work goes first. Which part of your own week would software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Price checking and reorder planning go first; they already trialled it on the paper towels line. Quarterly reports too. Calls with the reps would stay with me, because the reps like talking to a person and I'm good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Harlow would you worry about, and what would you tell Kenji that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, who sits next to me, has two kids and a husband out of work. I'd worry about her more than me. To Kenji I'd say we ride it out and we don't touch the mortgage plan, and I'd ask him to look for something with the city that isn't shifts.

say: I'd say **software** is taking the thinking work while owners keep the savings.
I'd call for **regulation** and union protection before buyers are cut.
think: Checking prices and reorders is **exactly** the work they'd hand to software.
If four buyers become two, I'm **not sure** I'd be kept.
do: Ask Dennis to teach me the new **reorder tool** this winter.
Pay down the **credit card** first and cancel eating out.
Keep the **supplier calls** as my own part of the job.
feel: **Frightened**, and ashamed of being the slow one on the team.
S1.quote: I've always been the one who knows how things work in our buying team, and now I'm the one asking the new graduate how to use the tool.
fieldNote: Admits **fear** because she has never used AI tools.
Sees the **supplier relationships** as the part software can't copy.
Worries first about a **colleague**, then herself.

steps.text: Ask Dennis to teach me the new reorder tool in the new year
Pay off the credit card before spending on anything else
Take the whole buying team to the union and ask for a job guarantee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario three is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a catastrophe and the government has to step in now. I'd tell people at work to join the union, because alone we're nothing. Online I'd be loud about it, which I never usually am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm finished at Harlow within two years. Everything I do is thinking work. We have almost no savings, so there's no cushion to retrain on, and there aren't many wholesale buying jobs in the area anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd sit down with Kenji and write out every bill. I'd go to the council and the union to ask what help exists. Then I'd look at anything with hands in it, like warehouse supervision, because I've walked that floor for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicky, honestly. My stomach drops. I can't see a plan, and everything I'd try needs money we don't have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what would you do in the first six months that you couldn't do with ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I could study and save. With two, I'd be applying for jobs while everyone else is fired at the same time. There's no time to be smart about it, only to ask for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your job is mostly desk and phone, with a monthly warehouse walk. What does robots-after-three-years mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The warehouse is where the robots come last, so that's my only hope, about three years after the desk goes. But I've never lifted anything heavy at Harlow and I'm forty-three. The three extra years are a gift, but they're not mine alone, because everyone else is going to want the same floor jobs.

say: I'd say this is a **catastrophe** and government must step in now.
I'd tell everyone to **join the union**, because alone we're nothing.
think: All my work is thinking work, so I could be **finished** within two years.
With **no savings** I can't pay for retraining.
do: Write out **every bill** with Kenji and cut to the bone.
Go to the **council and the union** to ask what help exists.
Look at **warehouse** supervisor jobs, where robots arrive later.
feel: **Panicky**, with a dropping stomach and no clear plan.
S2.quote: With ten years I could study and save. With two, I'd be applying for jobs while everyone else is fired at the same time.
fieldNote: The **short warning** is the whole problem: no cushion, no time.
Sees the **warehouse floor** as a lifeboat, but knows she is not physically ready.
Out of character: says she'd be **loud online**.

steps.text: Write out every bill with Kenji and cut to the bare minimum
Ask the council and the union what income help exists
Apply for warehouse supervisor jobs at the three depots nearby
Sign up every colleague at Harlow to the union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario four is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's serious but we have a little time, and the government should use it to plan help for families. I'd keep saying at work that nobody should be cut before there's a safety net. I'd probably still join the union rally, but with less panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm still worried, but I think I'd be one of the later ones. The big firms go first, and a small distributor like Harlow might stumble along a bit. Still, the money isn't there, so five years goes fast when you're paying a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save every spare coin into a cushion, even if it's tiny. I'd take the warehouse supervisor course through the council in the evenings, once Sora is in bed. I'd also learn the reorder tool slowly, so I'm not the last one in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but not frozen. I can see a path, though it's narrow, and it makes me tired to think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years is a different picture for you. What changes about the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything starts in the first year. I'd set up an automatic transfer even if it's only forty a month, and I'd put the course on the calendar. If I wait, I'll talk myself out of it, because that's how I am with new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell Mio and Sora anything differently with five years than with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my kids to be good with people and good with their hands, not only screens, and that Kenji and I are working on a plan. With two years I'd have no calm way to say anything. With five, I think I could still sound steady.

say: I'd say it's serious but there's **time** for the government to plan family help.
I'd keep saying nobody should be **cut** before a safety net exists.
think: I'd probably be one of the **later** ones, but the money isn't there.
Five years goes **fast** when you pay a mortgage every month.
do: Set up an **automatic transfer** of forty a month into a cushion.
Take the council's **warehouse supervisor** course in the evenings.
Learn the **reorder tool** slowly, before they make me.
feel: **Anxious** but not frozen; there is a narrow path.
S3.quote: I'd tell my kids to be good with people and good with their hands, not only screens
fieldNote: The extra time turns **panic into a plan**, but she distrusts herself to start.
Wants her children's careers to lean **hands-on**.
Chooses **small, steady** steps she can actually afford.

steps.text: Set up a forty-a-month automatic transfer into a cushion account
Enrol in the council's evening warehouse supervisor course
Practise the reorder tool for an hour each Friday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario five is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if people use it, and I'd want politicians planning now rather than panicking later. At work I'd keep my head down and do the job. I'd tell friends to push for retraining funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's still scary, but it's a worry for the end of my career, not tomorrow. By 2036 I'd be fifty-three, and the kids will be almost grown. I'd be working until sixty-five, so it still reaches me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay down the mortgage faster, even if it's small, and build real savings. I'd do the warehouse or logistics course in a few years, not now. And I'd try the AI tools bit by bit, because ten years gives me time to be bad at them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the others, but not calm. I get a flat tiredness, like when you know the rent will go up and there's nothing to do about it today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Does it feel like a threat at all, or more like something for your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More for the kids than me, partly. My job is exactly the kind that goes first, so ten years is only comfortable if I use it, and I know myself well enough to know I'd drift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask Calder, or the government, to do in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the government to fund retraining and income help the way they fund pensions, and Calder to promise no one is dropped without notice. I can't see them doing it. But asking costs nothing.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** if politicians plan now instead of panicking.
I'd tell friends to push for **retraining funds**.
think: It's the end of my career at stake, but I'd still be **working** past 60.
I'd probably **drift** and waste the time, knowing how I am.
do: Pay down the **mortgage** faster, even a little each month.
Do a **logistics** course in a few years, not right now.
Try the **AI tools** bit by bit while there is time.
feel: **Tired** and flat, like a rent rise nobody can stop today.
S4.quote: Ten years is only comfortable if I use it, and I know myself well enough to know I'd drift.
fieldNote: The decade lowers fear to **unease**, but she doubts her own follow-through.
Wants **retraining funded like pensions**, a progressive reflex.
Honest about her **resistance** to new things.

steps.text: Pay an extra thirty a month off the mortgage principal
Book a logistics course for 2029 once Sora is at secondary school
Write to the local councillor asking for funded retraining

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, with no doubt. It gives me no time and no savings, and I'd be on the street with everybody else. What would help is a proper income guarantee, a union that fights for us, and a retraining course that pays you while you do it. Plus an employer who gives notice, not a text message.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that I don't think the problem is machines. It's who owns them and who gets the savings. If the owners shared it, I'd be less afraid. I'd also say that people like me aren't stupid, we just never got shown the tools.

headlineQuote: I don't think the problem is machines. It's who owns them and who gets the savings.
portrait: **Amira Nakamura**, 43, buys cleaning supplies for Harlow Janitorial Supply in Eastgate, on **lower pay** with under a month saved.
Her **husband Kenji** drives buses; they have two children, Mio and Sora, and a variable-rate mortgage.
She has **never used AI tools** and fears being the slow one; she distrusts the private owners, Calder Holdings.
Her mood runs from **anxious** to **panicked** in the 2028 world, and she leans on unions and public help.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world, because she has no savings, no plan and no time.
whatWouldHelp: An **income guarantee**, notice from employers and a retraining course that **pays** while she studies.
